formulations.label: Tablets (scored)
formulations.note: The UK generic tablets checked are scored and can be divided into equal halves. The usual starting dose is 1 mg daily.

src.q: Glimepiride 2 mg tablets: 1 tablet contains Glimepiride 2 mg.
Glimepiride 3 mg tablets: 1 tablet contains Glimepiride 3 mg.
The tablet can be divided into equal halves.
The starting dose is 1 mg glimepiride per day.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes when diet, exercise and weight reduction alone are not adequate.

src.q: Glimepiride is indicated for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, when diet, physical exercise and weight reduction alone are not adequate.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK glimepiride 2 mg and 3 mg SmPCs checked.

items.t: Start 1 mg once daily. If needed, increase stepwise about every 1 to 2 weeks to 2, 3 or 4 mg daily. More than 4 mg helps only in exceptional cases. Maximum 6 mg daily.

src.q: The starting dose is 1 mg glimepiride per day.

in a stepwise manner with an interval of about 1 to 2 weeks between each step, to 2, 3 or 4 mg glimepiride per day. A dose of more than 4 mg glimepiride per day gives better results only in exceptional cases.
The maximum recommended dose is 6 mg glimepiride per day.

items.t: Added to maximum-dose metformin, or with insulin added to maximum-dose glimepiride: start the new medicine low and titrate under close medical supervision.

src.q: In patients not adequately controlled with the maximum daily dose of metformin, concomitant glimepiride therapy can be initiated if necessary.
The combination therapy should be initiated under close medical supervision.

items.t: Requirements may fall as control improves: consider timely dose reduction or stopping to avoid hypoglycaemia. Hypoglycaemia on 1 mg daily suggests diet alone may be enough.

src.q: To avoid hypoglycaemia timely dose reduction or cessation of therapy must therefore be considered.
If a patient has a hypoglycaemic reaction on 1 mg glimepiride daily, this indicates that they can be controlled by diet alone.

items.t: Switching from another oral hypoglycaemic: start at 1 mg; after long half-life agents a washout of a few days may be advisable.

src.q: In some cases, especially in antidiabetic medicines with a long half life (e.g. chlorpropamide), a wash out period of a few days is advisable

items.t: Missed dose: do not correct by increasing the next dose.

src.q: If a dose is forgotten, this should not be corrected by increasing the next dose.

items.t: Not recommended in children: no data under 8 years and insufficient data at 8 to 17 years.

src.q: There are no data available on the use of glimepiride in patients under 8 years of age.
The available data on safety and efficacy are insufficient in the paediatric population and therefore such use is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to glimepiride, other sulfonylureas, sulfonamides or any excipient.

src.q: hypersensitivity to glimepiride, other sulfonylureas or sulfonamides or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Type 1 diabetes; diabetic coma; ketoacidosis.

src.q: diabetes mellitus type 1, - diabetic coma, - ketoacidosis,

items.t: Severe renal or hepatic function disorders (change to insulin).

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: take shortly before or with a meal; irregular or skipped meals can cause hypoglycaemia. Severe or prolonged episodes need immediate medical treatment and sometimes hospital care; it may recur. Severe attacks can look like a stroke.

src.q: When meals are taken at irregular hours or skipped altogether, treatment with Glimepiride may lead to hypoglycaemia.
The clinical picture of a severe hypoglycaemic attack may resemble that of a stroke.
Severe hypoglycaemia or prolonged hypoglycaemia, only temporarily controlled by the usual amounts of sugar, require immediate medical treatment and occasionally hospitalisation.

items.t: Risk factors for hypoglycaemia: poor co-operation (more often elderly), poor nutrition or missed meals, diet changes, exercise without enough carbohydrate, alcohol, impaired renal function, serious liver dysfunction, some thyroid, pituitary or adrenal disorders, and interacting medicines.

src.q: unwillingness or (more commonly in elderly patients) incapacity of the patient to cooperate
consumption of alcohol, especially in combination with skipped meals, - impaired renal function, - serious liver dysfunction

items.t: Stress (accidents, acute operations, febrile infections): a temporary switch to insulin may be indicated.

src.q: In stress-situations (e.g. accidents, acute operations, infections with fever, etc.) a temporary switch to insulin may be indicated.

items.t: No experience in severe liver impairment or in dialysis patients.

src.q: No experience has been gained concerning the use of Glimepiride in patients with severe impairment of liver function or dialysis patients.

items.t: G6PD deficiency: risk of haemolytic anaemia; use with caution and consider a non-sulfonylurea alternative.

src.q: caution should be used in patients with G6PD-deficiency and a non-sulfonylurea alternative should be considered.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Glimepiride is metabolised by CYP2C9: inducers (e.g. rifampicin) and inhibitors (e.g. fluconazole) change its effect; fluconazole roughly doubles glimepiride exposure. Other medicines should only be taken with the doctor's knowledge.

src.q: Glimepiride is metabolized by cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9).
glimepiride AUC is increased approximately 2-fold by fluconazole
other medicinal products should only be taken with the knowledge (or at the prescription) of the doctor.

items.t: May increase glucose lowering (hypoglycaemia): insulin and other oral antidiabetics (e.g. metformin), salicylates, some long-acting sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolones, clarithromycin, coumarin anticoagulants, fibrates, ACE inhibitors, fluoxetine, MAOIs, allopurinol, miconazole, fluconazole, and others.

src.q: insulin and oral antidiabetic products, such as metformin, - salicylates and p-amino-salicylic acid
chloramphenicol, certain long acting sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolone antibiotics and clarithromycin, - coumarin anticoagulants
fibrates, - ACE inhibitors, - fluoxetine, MAO-inhibitors, - allopurinol, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone
miconazole, fluconazole

items.t: May weaken glucose lowering (raised glucose): oestrogens and progestogens, thiazide diuretics, glucocorticoids, thyroid-stimulating agents, phenothiazines, adrenaline and sympathomimetics, long-term laxatives, phenytoin, rifampicin, acetazolamide, and others.

src.q: oestrogens and progestogens, - saluretics, thiazide diuretics, - thyroid stimulating agents, glucocorticoids
adrenaline and sympathicomimetics
laxatives (long term use)

items.t: Beta-blockers (and clonidine, reserpine, H2 antagonists): may increase or weaken the effect; beta-blockers may reduce or abolish the warning signs of hypoglycaemia.

src.q: H2 antagonists, beta blockers, clonidine and reserpine may lead to either potentiation or weakening of the blood glucose lowering effect.
the signs of adrenergic counterregulation to hypoglycaemia may be reduced or absent.

items.t: Alcohol: may increase or weaken the effect unpredictably. Coumarin anticoagulants: glimepiride may increase or weaken their effect.

src.q: Alcohol intake may potentiate or weaken the hypoglycaemic action of glimepiride in an unpredictable fashion.
Glimepiride may either potentiate or weaken the effects of coumarin derivatives.

items.t: Colesevelam (not in this tool's list): give glimepiride at least 4 hours before.

src.q: glimepiride should be administered at least 4 hours prior to colesevelam.

items.t: Severe renal function disorders: contraindicated; change to insulin. The SmPC gives no numeric threshold. Impaired renal function increases hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.
impaired renal function

items.t: No experience in dialysis patients.

src.q: No experience has been gained concerning the use of Glimepiride in patients with severe impairment of liver function or dialysis patients.

items.t: Severe hepatic function disorders: contraindicated; change to insulin. Serious liver dysfunction increases hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.
serious liver dysfunction

items.t: SmPC: should not be used at any stage of pregnancy (animal reproductive toxicity). If planning pregnancy or pregnant, switch to insulin as soon as possible.

src.q: Consequently, glimepiride should not be used during the whole pregnancy.
In case of treatment by glimepiride, if the patient plans to become pregnant or if a pregnancy is discovered, the treatment should be switched as soon as possible to insulin therapy.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; sulfonylureas are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: breastfeeding is advised against (other sulfonylureas pass into milk; risk of hypoglycaemia in the infant).

src.q: As other sulfonylureas are excreted in human milk and because there is a risk of hypoglycaemia in nursing infants, breast-feeding is advised against during treatment with glimepiride.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: No fertility data. Patients considering pregnancy should tell their doctor.

src.q: No data on fertility is available.
Patients who consider pregnancy should inform their physician.

items.t: The SmPC lists no very common or common reactions. Listed as rare: hypoglycaemia (may be severe and hard to correct), taste disturbance, alopecia, weight gain, and blood count changes.

src.q: Rare: hypoglycaemia. These hypoglycaemic reactions mostly occur immediately, may be severe and are not always easy to correct.
Rare: dysgeusia.
Rare: alopecia.
Rare: weight gain.

items.t: Transient visual disturbances, especially when starting, from changes in blood glucose (frequency not known).

src.q: Not known: visual disturbances, transient, may occur especially on initiation of treatment, due to changes in blood glucose levels.

items.t: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia: needs immediate medical treatment, sometimes in hospital; may recur.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia or prolonged hypoglycaemia, only temporarily controlled by the usual amounts of sugar, require immediate medical treatment and occasionally hospitalisation.

items.t: Blood disorders (rare: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, haemolytic anaemia, pancytopenia; not known: severe thrombocytopenia with purpura).

src.q: Rare: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis, erythropenia, haemolytic anaemia and pancytopenia, which are in general reversible upon discontinuation of medication.
Not known: severe thrombocytopenia with platelet count less than 10,000/μl and thrombocytopenic purpura.

items.t: Very rare: hypersensitivity that may progress to breathlessness, low blood pressure and shock; hepatitis and hepatic failure; low sodium.

src.q: Very rare: leukocytoclaslic vasculitis, mild hypersensitivity reactions that may develop into serious reactions with dyspnoea, fall in blood pressure and sometimes shock.
Very rare: hepatic function abnormal (e.g. with cholestasis and jaundice), hepatitis and hepatic failure.

items.t: Blood and urine glucose regularly; HbA1c recommended.

src.q: Treatment with Glimepiride requires regular monitoring of glucose levels in blood and urine. In addition determination of the proportion of glycosylated haemoglobin is recommended.

items.t: Liver function and blood counts (especially white cells and platelets) regularly.

src.q: Regular hepatic and haematological monitoring (especially leucocytes and thrombocytes) are required during treatment with Glimepiride.

items.t: Review dose as control improves; reduce or stop if hypoglycaemia occurs.

src.q: To avoid hypoglycaemia timely dose reduction or cessation of therapy must therefore be considered.

items.t: Once daily shortly before or during a substantial breakfast (or the first main meal). Swallow with some liquid.

src.q: It is recommended that this dose be taken shortly before or during a substantial breakfast or - if none is taken - shortly before or during the first main meal.
Tablets should be swallowed whole with some liquid.

items.t: Take shortly before or with a meal and do not skip meals; know the signs of low blood sugar. Sugar treats it; artificial sweeteners do not.

src.q: Glimepiride must be taken shortly before or during a meal.
Symptoms can almost always be promptly controlled by immediate intake carbohydrates (sugar). Artificial sweeteners have no effect.

items.t: Take precautions to avoid low blood sugar when driving, especially with reduced awareness of warning signs or frequent episodes.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia whilst driving.

items.t: Take other medicines only with your doctor's knowledge.

src.q: other medicinal products should only be taken with the knowledge (or at the prescription) of the doctor.
